title: Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries: a systematic review, qualitative analysis and meta-analysis
authors: Lauersen JB, Andersen TE, Andersen LB
population: Participants aged 12-40 years in six RCTs of strength-training-based primary injury prevention (five from Europe, one from Africa); 7,738 participants with 177 acute or overuse injuries
findings: Six studies analysed five different interventions with four distinct outcomes; 7,738 participants aged 12-40 years sustained 177 acute or overuse injuries.
Cluster-adjusted intention-to-treat RR 0.338 (0.238-0.480), consistent across robustness tests; strength of evidence rated high; no publication bias found.
A 10% increase in strength training volume reduced injury risk by more than four percentage points.
Authors report the included studies were generally well designed, had high compliance and were safe; increasing strength training volume and intensity were associated with injury risk reduction.
limitations: Only six trials and 177 injuries; sport-general populations with considerable differences between interventions, so the dose-response is exploratory (post-hoc meta-regression); not running-specific.
implications: Support progressive increases in strength volume and intensity over the year rather than a flat dose, within the 2-3 session per week ceiling.
Keep strength in the plan year-round, not only in a pre-season block.
Do not convert the 10% volume to four percentage points figure into a formula; use it as directional support only.

verification.notes: Crossref and Europe PMC re-fetched. Removed unsupported 'largely team sports and youth' descriptor; age range 12-40 is in the abstract.
